source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, ICLR - Table 1 re-read with layout (ar5iv HTML table)
finding: Table 1 row labels are now fixed. Rows are 0-shot, 0-shot CoT, 5-shot CoT, Ours (self-generated exemplars). The 75.0 value is the 0-shot row for GPT-3.5-turbo, not 5-shot CoT. The a33/c18 conflict is settled: c18 was wrong.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT3.5-turbo / text-davinci-003 / PaLM2: 0-shot 75.0 / 14.8 / 60.8; 0-shot CoT 75.8 / 50.3 / 78.2; 5-shot CoT 76.7 / 54.0 / 80.7; Ours 77.8 / 61.0 (dagger) / 81.7. MATH, GPT3.5-turbo / PaLM2: 0-shot 33.0 / 27.1; 0-shot CoT 33.9 / 29.8; 5-shot CoT 34.9 / 34.3; Ours 37.3 / 34.8. Gain of Ours over 5-shot CoT: +1.1, +7.0, +1.0 on GSM8K; +2.4, +0.5 on MATH.
limits: 5-shot CoT here uses fixed manual exemplars, not retrieved ones. The dagger on 61.0 marks text-davinci models given an in-context demo of how to self-generate. Gains over 5-shot CoT are small (0.5 to 2.4 points) except on davinci-003.
agent_relevance: Use these corrected labels. Self-generated analogues beat fixed few-shot by 0.5 to 7 points; the gain is real but small for strong models.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) - Table 4 (GSM8K by model scale) and Sections 6.3-6.4, generating vs retrieving exemplars
finding: Retrieved exemplars (SBERT top-5 from the GSM8K train set) beat self-generated exemplars for small models. Self-generation wins only for the largest models, and only by a few points. The crossover sits between text-davinci-001 and -002 (tie at -002, win at -003).
numbers: GSM8K accuracy, curie-001 / davinci-001 / davinci-002 / davinci-003: 0-shot 2/6/13/14; 0-shot CoT 2/6/22/50; 5-shot fixed CoT 2/10/43/54; 5-shot retrieved CoT 3/11/47/57; Ours (self-generated) 2/9/48/61. Self-generated minus retrieved: -1, -2, +1, +4 points.
quote: retrieval typically needs labeled exemplars and involves a complex additional retrieval step
limits: Single-run percentages on one dataset; the davinci-003 value includes the in-context demo. Retrieved exemplars come from a labeled train set of the same task, which the agent may not have. Tested only on 2022-era models.
agent_relevance: Self-generation needs a model that already knows related problems. For a store the agent built itself and a frontier model, expect self-generation and retrieval to be close; retrieval wins where the store holds problems the model has not seen.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) - Table 2 (Codeforces) and Table 3 (BIG-Bench)
finding: On Codeforces the gain from self-generated exemplars shrinks from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4. Adding self-generated knowledge helps more than exemplars alone.
numbers: Codeforces Acc@1 / Acc@10, GPT3.5-turbo-16k: 0-shot 8/24; 0-shot CoT 9/27; 3-shot CoT 11/27; Ours exemplars 13/25; Ours knowledge+exemplars 15/29. GPT-4: 16/30; 16/29; 17/31; 17/32; 19/37. BIG-Bench word sorting (GPT-3.5): 0-shot CoT 66.8, 3-shot CoT 67.6, Ours 68.4.
limits: Acc@1 gain of exemplars-only over 3-shot CoT: +2 for GPT-3.5, 0 for GPT-4. Small test sets; BIG-Bench tasks evaluated twice and averaged.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 hint: the benefit of self-generated analogues falls as the base model gets stronger, at least on code.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025/2026) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing reasoning capability in LLMs via RL
finding: The authors report that few-shot prompting consistently hurts their reasoning model and advise zero-shot. If this holds for current reasoning models, injecting retrieved exemplars at task start is a risk, not a free gain.
numbers: No table; qualitative statement in the prompting-engineering note.
quote: Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance.
limits: One model family; no number given for the drop. Not a retrieval study. Exemplars are fixed, not retrieved by structure.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 and gap 4: for strong reasoning models, give the retrieved case as a hint at the stuck point, not as a few-shot block at the start, and measure with and without.

source: Chen, Chen, Sun & Zhang (2026) Analogical Deep Research (CANA), arXiv 2607.13602 - Tables 1 and 3
finding: Commercial deep-research agents almost never find a useful historical analogy. Storing events as structural decompositions (preconditions, chain, mechanism, outcome) and retrieving on that raises analogy quality, mostly for weaker models.
numbers: MDS score (GPT-5.4 judge), gpt-5.4-mini: Direct 3.05, Summarizing 3.59, Self-reflection 3.34, CANA 4.01. sonnet-4-6: Direct 2.24, Summarizing 3.91, Self-reflection 4.11, CANA 4.17 (saturated). qwen3-8b: Direct 1.76, Self-reflection 3.94. ADR-bench, 10 historical events (22 hidden factors): Gemini DR 0/22, ChatGPT DR 0/22, Qwen DR 0/22, MiroFlow(GPT-5.4) 1/22; CANA(Sonnet-4.5) 13/22, CANA(GPT-5.4) 7/22, CANA(Qwen3-8B) 1/22. Text: retrieval through decomposed representation improves more than 10 percent over self-reflection.
quote: LLM agents are poor at finding analogies because they match on surface features rather than underlying mechanisms.
limits: Single preprint, small benchmark (15 events), LLM judge, authors' own method. Task is analogue generation and use, not retrieval from a large store. The gain of CANA over self-reflection shrinks with model strength (+0.67 for gpt-5.4-mini, +0.06 for sonnet-4-6). The cost of the decomposition step was not isolated.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 2 (store structure, not surface) and gap 9 (the scaffold matters less as the model gets stronger).

source: Jung et al. (2026) Cross-Pollination Retrieval, arXiv 2610.25678 - Table 2 and Appendix H (LLM reranker details)
finding: A candidate pool followed by an LLM tournament rerank finds structurally useful papers far better than any single-vector retriever, and the cost per query is known: about 20 LLM calls.
numbers: CPR-eval 1,300 queries, 151 candidates each (1 positive, 150 hard negatives). Recall@10: best of 11 retrievers 0.26 (chance 0.07); LLM reranker (MiMo-V2.6-Pro) 0.81; fine-tuned retrievers up to 0.70. Reranker: 8 group calls + 2 selection calls + 10 scoring calls + tie-break = 20.2 calls per query, $91.78 total, $0.071 per query. Positive reached the final ten for 1,058 queries; eliminated in round 2 for 134 and in round 1 for 108 (so 8.3 percent lost at the first cut from 151 to 40).
limits: Pool is fixed at 151, not a whole corpus; the authors say a full corpus is harder and that reranker Recall@10 assumes the pool holds the positive. Papers, not agent memory. Single preprint.
agent_relevance: The nearest published test of 'cheap filter, then LLM structural rerank'. It shows the rerank stage works and what it costs. It does not compare against one-stage top-k at equal tokens, so gap 1 stays open.

source: Su et al. (2025) BRIGHT, ICLR - Section 5.1 reranking, Table 3, Table 47
finding: Reranking the top 10 or top 100 with GPT-4 lifts reasoning-intensive retrieval a little; reranking more candidates adds almost nothing. A cross-encoder trained on MS MARCO makes it worse. Reasoning-expanded queries help more than reranking.
numbers: Average nDCG@10 over BRIGHT. BM25 base 14.3: MiniLM top10 13.1, top100 8.3; Gemini top10 15.7; GPT-4 top10 17.4, top100 17.0. Google base 19.5: MiniLM 16.0 / 9.4; Gemini 20.1; GPT-4 21.5 (k=10), 22.6 (k=100). LLM-written reasoning as query: up to +12.2 points. Downstream GPT-4o, TheoremQA theorems: none 82.1, random doc 85.0, oracle doc 89.7.
limits: Rerank depth 10 vs 100 changes GPT-4 by -0.4 (BM25) and +1.1 (Google) points. The final result still depends on the underlying retrieval system. Web-scale corpora; GPT-4-0125 era models.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: with a decent first stage, a shortlist of about 10 to 20 is enough for the LLM rerank; widening to 100 is not worth the tokens. Gap 1: rewriting the query as a reasoning trace (one cheap call) is a strong competitor to reranking.

source: Li et al. (2024) Retrieval augmented generation or long-context LLMs? (Self-Route), arXiv 2407.16833 - Table 1, Section 4
finding: Stuffing the whole context beats plain top-k RAG on average, but RAG is far cheaper. A hybrid that lets the model say 'unanswerable from these chunks' and falls back to the full context nearly matches stuffing at 38 to 61 percent of the tokens.
numbers: Averages over 9 long-context QA and summarization sets, Contriever, k=5. Gemini-1.5-Pro: LC 49.70, RAG 37.33, Self-Route 46.41, 76.78 percent answered by RAG, 38.39 percent of tokens. GPT-4O: LC 48.67, RAG 32.60, Self-Route 48.89 at 61.40 percent of tokens. GPT-3.5-Turbo: LC 32.07, RAG 30.33, Self-Route 35.32 at 38.85 percent. Cost minimum near k=5 on average, k=1 on extractive sets.
limits: Knowledge QA over documents, not analogy retrieval. The text quotes GPT-4O 46.83 vs LC 47.04, which differs from the table average, so treat small gaps as approximate. Predictions of RAG and LC are identical for over 60 percent of queries.
agent_relevance: The nearest equal-cost style comparison for gap 1: a cheap retrieval pass with a self-declared escape hatch captures most of the long-context accuracy. 'Retrieve first, stuff only if the model says it cannot answer' is worth testing on analogue retrieval.

source: Suzgun, Yuksekgonul, Bianchi, Jurafsky & Zou (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet, arXiv 2504.07952 - Table 1, Table 2, Section 4.3
finding: With frontier-model APIs (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o), memory kept as short curated strategy notes with retrieval beats raw retrieval of past cases in most rows, and both beat appending the full history. Retrieval of raw cases can confuse the weaker model.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, baseline / retrieval only (DR) / curated no retrieval (DC-Cu) / retrieve+synthesize (DC-RS): AIME 2024 23.3 / 43.3 / 50.0 / 46.7; AIME 2025 6.7 / 23.3 / 36.7 / 30.0; GPQA-Diamond 59.6 / 63.6 / 61.1 / 68.7. GPT-4o: AIME 2024 20.0 / 26.7 / 36.7 / 40.0; GPQA 57.1 / 55.1 / 58.1 / 57.1. Full-history appending (FH) on AIME 2024: Sonnet 26.7 vs DC 50.0; GPT-4o 6.7 vs DC-RS 40.0 (baseline 20.0).
quote: retrieval can, in some cases, introduce confusion, especially if suboptimal examples are recalled
limits: Small question sets (30 per AIME year, 198 GPQA). FH uses far more tokens, so it is not an equal-token control. 2024 vintage models. Memory is built from the same task stream.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 2: distilled notes plus selective retrieval beat both raw-trace retrieval and context stuffing on frontier-API models. GPT-4o AIME 2024: stuffing (6.7) is worse than no memory (20.0).

source: Wang, Mao, Fried & Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory, arXiv 2409.07429 - Mind2Web Tables 3 and 6; WebArena Table 5
finding: Memory stored as abstract, example-stripped workflows beats retrieving the most relevant concrete past examples on Mind2Web cross-task. The authors say concrete examples bias element choice. On WebArena, LLM abstraction and rule-based deduplication tie.
numbers: Mind2Web cross-task, step SR / element accuracy: AWM (gpt-3.5) 34.6 / 39.0 vs Synapse (retrieved examples, gpt-3.5) 30.6 / 34.0; AWM (gpt-4) 45.1 / 50.6 vs MindAct (gpt-4) 36.2 / 41.6. Rule-based induction AWM-rule 43.4 / 49.5 vs LM-based 45.1 / 50.6. WebArena gpt-4 total SR: rule 35.6, LM 35.5; steps 6.3 vs 5.9. Text: relative gains 24.6 and 51.1 percent over baselines.
limits: Web-navigation actions, not analogy; abstraction here removes example-specific values, not relational structure. Task SR on Mind2Web stays at 2 to 5 percent, so step SR is the usable signal. The abstraction and the retrieval method differ at once.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 2: abstracted memory entries outperform retrieved raw examples by 4 points of step SR with the same model, but not when a simple dedupe is used on WebArena.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank, arXiv 2509.25140 - Table 1 (WebArena), Section C.1 (number of retrieved experiences)
finding: Distilled reasoning items (title, description, content) beat raw-trajectory memory (Synapse) and workflow memory (AWM). Retrieving one item is best; adding more lowers the success rate.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-flash, WebArena overall SR: No Memory 40.5; Synapse 42.1; AWM 44.1; ReasoningBank 48.8; ReasoningBank+MaTTS 51.8. Retrieved-count ablation on the plotted subset: no memory 39.0; 1 item 49.7; 2 items 46.5; 3 items 45.5; 4 items 44.4. Text: Synapse and AWM fail to give gains or degrade on the cross-website Multi subset.
quote: the relevance and quality of memory are more crucial than sheer quantity
limits: Figure text was interleaved in the extraction; the ablation panel appears to be one domain (39.0 equals the Shopping no-memory value), not the overall figure. Top-1 is the final injected set, not a cheap-stage shortlist. One model for the ablation.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the set shown to the solver should be small (1 to 2). The cheap stage can be wider, but what is injected should not be.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners, AAAI - Fig. 5 text, Table 3, Section 5.6
finding: Abstract insights and retrieved successful trajectories contribute differently by task. Retrieval keyed on task similarity beats retrieval keyed on the current reasoning step, and random retrieval is close to no memory. Insights are made by comparing a failed and a successful trajectory of the same task.
numbers: HotpotQA SR: ReAct 28.0; hand-crafted insights 32.0; insights with reflections 29.0; gpt-3.5 insights 32.0; ExpeL 39.0. Insights-only vs retrieve-only: HotpotQA 36 vs 31 percent; ALFWorld 50 vs 55 percent; WebShop 37 vs 38. ALFWorld ablation: ReAct 40.0; reasoning-similarity retrieval 48.5; random sampled 42.5; ExpeL task-similarity 59.0. Extracting insights from the few-shot examples alone gave no gain over ReAct.
limits: ReAct-style text environments, GPT-3.5/4 era, error bars around 1 to 2 points. Reasoning-step retrieval changes the few-shot during a trajectory, which the authors blame for instability. No ablation of paired comparison against single-trajectory insight extraction.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: re-retrieving at each step on the model's own reasoning text was worse than one task-level retrieval in ALFWorld, the opposite of the HippoSpark story; the keys differ (step text vs a stuck-state description). Gap 3: the compare-fail-vs-success operation is in the pipeline but not isolated, so there is only an indirect hint.

source: Liu et al. (2026) HippoSpark, arXiv 2606.29929 - Table 2, Section 4.4, Appendix G.2.1
finding: Retrieval that fires when the model says it is stuck (state-level, on-demand) beats task-level trajectory and reasoning-bank retrieval. Task-level trajectory memory often falls below the vanilla baseline. Firing too often is a bad sign: after about five calls gains turn unstable or negative.
numbers: Overall score (AIME24, AIME25, GPQA-Diamond, BigCodeBench). GPT-5.4-mini: Vanilla 0.326; Trajectory Exp. 0.255; ReasoningBank 0.306; Ours without experience 0.409; Ours with experience 0.483. Qwen3-14B: Vanilla 0.283; Trajectory Exp. 0.261; Ours without 0.330; Ours 0.368. Of 300 AIME instances (Qwen3-32B), 10.67 percent triggered no retrieval and already reached 71.88 percent accuracy without experience. Output tokens, CoT vs +Transition: 3041 to 3414.
quote: retrieval is guided by the wrong formulation and may reinforce an unproductive direction
limits: Single preprint. The state-assessment and verification steps give most of the lift (0.326 to 0.409 on GPT-5.4-mini before any experience), so experience adds 0.074 there and 0.038 on Qwen3-14B. Table layout is garbled for Qwen3-32B, so that block is not quoted. Math, science and code, not analogy.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a trigger rule that works in this paper is 'retrieve when the move generator reports an unclear next step, query with the current situation and local goal, cap at about 5 calls'. High retrieval counts flag a wrongly framed state, which suggests re-framing before retrieving again.

source: Liu et al. (2026) HippoSpark - Appendix G.1 (coverage bottleneck, GPQA Biology)
finding: When the memory is small the best match is weak and experience stops helping. Biology had only 20 to 28 experience items and its top-1 similarity stayed low.
numbers: Experience items (Qwen3-32B / 14B / GPT-5.4-mini): Biology 20 / 28 / 20; Physics 78 / 124 / 94; Chemistry 112 / 152 / 124. Mean top-1 retrieval score on Qwen3-32B: Biology 0.676 (max 0.760), Physics 0.706 (max 0.788), Chemistry 0.751 (max 0.879).
limits: Similarity is an embedding score on a card trigger field, not a judgment of analogy. Three domains, one paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: coverage caps the gain. An agent with a few dozen items will often hold no true analogue, and the top-1 score is a usable cue that none exists. Log the top-1 score and skip injection below a threshold set on a dev set.

source: Xiao et al. (2026) RA-RFT, arXiv 2606.13680 - Table 2, Table 3, Figure 3
finding: Plain embedding retrieval of traces is no better than a random trace from the same problem type. Only a retriever trained on LLM-judged reasoning relevance helps. Before training, adding a retrieved trace lowers accuracy because the model is distracted by it.
numbers: Qwen3-1.7B average@32 over AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, BrUMO25 (Avg): SFT 39.7; RA-SFT 40.5; GRPO 43.3; RA-RFT 47.4. Retriever table (Avg): Qwen3-Embedding-4B 38.5 (R@1 2.3); same, fine-tuned 40.5 (R@1 14.7); Reason-ModernColBERT 40.7 (R@1 7.2); fine-tuned 47.4 (R@1 43.5); random trace 37.6. Step-0 accuracy of the retrieval-augmented policy is below GRPO on all four benchmarks.
limits: Training-time retrieval inside reinforcement fine-tuning of small Qwen3 models; not a prompting-only agent. k=1. Relevance labels come from a GPT-4o judge over all pairs.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and gap 1: start-of-task retrieval with surface similarity can hurt, and an LLM relevance judge on candidate pairs is the part that does the work. Off-the-shelf embeddings had R@1 of 2.3 percent for gold reasoning-relevant traces.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Active retrieval augmented generation (FLARE), EMNLP - Section 6.2
finding: Retrieving only when the next sentence has low-confidence tokens beats retrieving every sentence. There is an optimum share of steps that retrieve; beyond it, extra retrieval is noise.
numbers: Triggering retrieval for 40 to 80 percent of sentences usually gave good performance across datasets. On 2WikiMultihopQA performance plateaus above 60 percent retrieval; on StrategyQA it drops when retrieval exceeds 50 percent. Forward-looking (next sentence) queries beat past-context queries.
quote: unnecessary retrieval can introduce noise and impede the original generation process
limits: text-davinci-003 and knowledge QA. Confidence is the token probability, which a closed API may not expose.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a confidence-triggered rule retrieves for about half of the steps. For an agent without logits, a verbalised 'I do not know the next move' flag plays the same role (as in HippoSpark).

source: Mallen et al. (2023) When not to trust language models (PopQA, adaptive retrieval), ACL - Section 6
finding: Retrieve only for the cases the model is unlikely to know, using a threshold tuned on a dev set. Large models need retrieval less, small models almost always. Always-retrieve is worse and slower.
numbers: Adaptive Retrieval on PopQA: GPT-3 davinci-003 retrieves for about 40 percent of questions with BM25; GPT-neox 20B does not retrieve on more than 20 percent of questions; gains are small for models under 10B parameters, which almost always retrieve. Latency and API cost fall when retrieval is skipped.
quote: the retrieved context can be misleading
limits: Entity popularity as the trigger signal is specific to factual QA. The paper warns that the retrieved context can be misleading for popular entities.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the trigger threshold shifts with model strength. The same agent scaffold should retrieve less often as the model improves; tune the threshold per model.

source: Asai et al. (2023) Self-RAG, ICLR 2024 - Section 5.2 ablation (Table 3a)
finding: Learned on-demand retrieval beats always retrieving the top passage. Using top passages regardless of relevance causes a large drop on PopQA and ASQA.
numbers: Ablation (PopQA / PubHealth / ASQA), 50k-example 7B model: No retrieval 24.7 / 73.0; Hard constraints (retrieve whenever the model says yes) 28.3 / 72.6; Retrieve top-1 always 41.8 / 73.1 / 28.6; Remove ISSUP 44.1 / 73.2 / 30.6. The full-model row was not recoverable from the text extraction.
limits: Needs a trained critic model; knowledge QA. PubHealth barely changes with any setting.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: supports a gate on retrieval and a relevance critique before injecting. A prompt-only version (ask whether the retrieved case is relevant and how it maps) is the cheap stand-in.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the middle, TACL - Section 2 and Table 1
finding: Stuffing many documents into the context lowers accuracy and the position of the answer matters. With 20 or 30 documents GPT-3.5 can do worse than with none.
numbers: Multi-document QA, closed-book vs oracle: GPT-3.5-Turbo 56.1 vs 88.3; Claude-1.3 48.3 vs 76.1; LongChat-13B 35.0 vs 83.4. Accuracy can drop by more than 20 percent when the relevant document is in the middle; at 20 and 30 documents the worst case falls below closed-book 56.1.
quote: performance in 20- and 30-document settings is lower than performance without any input documents
limits: 2023 models; newer long-context models have improved on position bias. Wikipedia passages with one gold passage.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: raw stuffing of memory into the prompt is a poor baseline for equal tokens. Order and prune the shortlist; put the best case at the start or end.

source: Jin, Yoon, Han & Arik (2024) Long-context LLMs meet RAG, arXiv 2410.05983
finding: For many long-context LLMs, quality first rises then falls as more passages are retrieved. Hard negatives from strong retrievers cause the fall. Reordering retrieved passages helps without training.
numbers: Qualitative in the abstract and introduction: an inverted-U in the number of retrieved passages, and stronger retrievers can give more confusing hard negatives.
quote: quality of generated output initially improves first, but then subsequently declines as the number of retrieved passages increases
limits: Knowledge QA; per-model numbers are in figures not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the cheap stage should not be widened for its own sake. Near-miss analogues (same surface, wrong structure) are exactly the hard negatives that hurt, so a structural rerank is needed before injection.

source: Dhuliawala et al. (2023) Chain-of-Verification reduces hallucination, arXiv 2309.11495
finding: Having the model plan short check questions and answer them independently of the draft cuts false items. The independent (two-step and factored) variants beat the joint variant, because the model does not copy its own error.
numbers: Wikidata list questions, Llama 65B precision: few-shot 0.17; CoVe joint 0.29; two-step 0.36; factored 0.32.
limits: Fact lists, not analogy mapping. Extra calls scale with the number of claims.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: the transferable idea is to verify a proposed analogy with independent, narrow questions ('does role X map to Y?') rather than ask the model to re-judge its whole answer. No test on analogies exists.

source: Jung et al. (2026) Cross-Pollination Retrieval - Section 3.2 (analogy judgment and second-call verification) and Appendix C
finding: A two-call design keeps analogies honest at dataset-building time: one LLM call extracts the object mapping and shared relations; a second call checks that the target really uses the source's contribution and rejects same-problem, background-only or unsupported-mapping cases.
numbers: The first judgment discards about 91 percent of cross-topic citation pairs. Second-call verification agrees with a human annotator on 50 items: 0.92 agreement, Cohen's kappa 0.84 (half accepted, half rejected). Usefulness rating of positives: 25 items, 0.92, kappa 0.84; of candidates: 25 items, 0.96, kappa 0.92.
limits: Human check is by one author on 50 items. Built for data construction, not live agent use; token cost of the verifier is not reported separately.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a concrete cheap pattern: force an explicit mapping (objects and relations) then a second call with a reject taxonomy. Rejecting 91 percent of surface-different pairs also shows how rare true analogues are (gap 6).

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) counterfactual letter-string analogies (arXiv 2402.08955); Stevenson et al. (2025) generalising analogy solving like children (arXiv 2411.02348)
finding: LLM analogy accuracy falls when the content is unfamiliar (permuted alphabets, Greek, symbol alphabets) while humans hold steady. So familiarity of the surface vocabulary raises LLM analogy performance. Whether a familiar named structure helps retrieval is not tested.
numbers: Lewis & Mitchell: accuracy over 1,876 samples, humans 0.753 [0.734, 0.773], GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452; 136 human participants. Stevenson et al.: each LLM fell significantly from Latin to Greek to Symbol alphabet (Bonferroni p<.001 for all but Llama-3.1 405B, p=.012 for Latin to Greek); adults and children did not.
limits: Letter-string puzzles, not memory retrieval. Familiar here means familiar symbols, not a familiar relational schema, so it is only an indirect hint for gap 8.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. Indirect hint: do not assume a named pattern in the key will transfer to retrieval; test it. Keys written in the model's usual vocabulary are safer.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts, NeurIPS - Sections 3.1, 5, 6
finding: A problem-distiller turns the task into its key variables and constraints, then a retrieved high-level template is instantiated. Removing the distiller or the meta-buffer lowers accuracy, most on Game of 24 and Checkmate-in-One. Small models gain a lot from retrieved templates.
numbers: Reported with GPT-4: 11 percent on Game of 24, 20 percent on Geometric Shapes, 51 percent on Checkmate-in-One over Meta-prompting; 79.4 percent over GPT-4 on Game of 24. Ablations (w/o problem-distiller, w/o meta-buffer) are bar charts only, showing a decline for Llama3-70B and GPT-4. BoT+Llama3-8B has the potential to surpass single Llama3-70B.
limits: Exact ablation numbers are in figures, not extracted. Templates are code-like and tasks repeat a fixed type (puzzles), so a template exists for most test items, which inflates the coverage assumption. The authors admit limited gains for creative problems.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 9: supports retrieving on a distilled problem description and storing abstract templates. Weaker models gain most from retrieved templates, matching the Yasunaga crossover. Coverage by task type is an assumption the agent cannot make.
